summary: Haggai 1 opens with a dated message in the second year of Darius, addressed to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. The people say it is not yet time to build Yahweh’s house, but the message challenges them for living in paneled houses while that house lies waste. After Haggai connects their disappointing harvests and wages with that neglect, the leaders and the remnant obey, hear Yahweh’s assurance, and begin work.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the book’s main issue: the unfinished temple is not a background detail but the public sign of the community’s misplaced priorities. It also shows the book’s basic movement from rebuke to response to encouragement.

context.author: The messages are attributed to Haggai the prophet; the book does not name the person who arranged them in final form.
context.audience: Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people of Judah, called to resume work on Yahweh’s house.
context.date: The chapter dates this message and the beginning of work to the sixth month of the second year of Darius I, in 520 BCE.
context.setting: Judah under Persian rule, with Zerubbabel as governor and Joshua as high priest. Babylonian destruction and exile lie behind the community’s situation.
context.literaryForm: Dated prophetic message with a report of the people’s response.

outline.heading: The dated word to Judah’s leaders
outline.note: The chapter locates the message under Darius and names Haggai, Zerubbabel, and Joshua.

outline.heading: The delay is challenged
outline.note: The people say the time has not come to build Yahweh’s house, while their own paneled houses stand in contrast to the house that lies waste.

outline.heading: Consider the disappointing results
outline.note: The message asks the people to consider their ways and describes work that produces little lasting satisfaction.

outline.heading: Build the house
outline.note: The repeated call to consider leads to a concrete command: bring wood and build the house.

outline.heading: The drought explained
outline.note: Yahweh links the small harvests and drought to the neglected house and the people’s attention to their own houses.

outline.heading: The people obey and begin work
outline.note: Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant obey, fear Yahweh, receive the promise “I am with you,” and come to work on the house.

keyVerses.text: “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies waste?
keyVerses.why: This question names the chapter’s central contrast between private comfort and the neglected house of Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: You have sown much, and bring in little. You eat, but you don’t have enough. You drink, but you aren’t filled with drink. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm; and he who earns wages earns wages to put them into a bag with holes in it.’
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the vivid picture of effort without enough return, which the chapter asks the people to consider.

keyVerses.text: Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house. I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified,” says Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: The command turns the rebuke into a specific act of rebuilding, with Yahweh’s stated pleasure and glory in view.

keyVerses.text: Then Haggai, Yahweh’s messenger, spoke Yahweh’s message to the people, saying, “I am with you,” says Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: This short assurance follows the people’s obedience and prepares for the work that begins in the next verse.

questions.question: When does this chapter take place?
questions.answer: The chapter dates the first message to the first day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius the king. It later dates the beginning of work to the twenty-fourth day of that same month. These events take place in Judah under Persian rule in 520 BCE.

questions.question: Who are Zerubbabel and Joshua in this chapter?
questions.answer: Zerubbabel is called the son of Shealtiel and governor of Judah. Joshua is called the son of Jehozadak and the high priest. The message is addressed to these leaders, and they later obey with the remnant of the people.

questions.question: What does “Yahweh’s house” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “Yahweh’s house” is the temple in Jerusalem that the people are being told to rebuild. The contrast is between that house lying waste and the people living in their own paneled houses. The chapter does not criticize having ordinary houses in general; it criticizes this community’s neglect of the temple work.

questions.question: What does “Consider your ways” ask the people to do?
questions.answer: The phrase appears twice, before and after the description of their poor returns. It asks the people to pay attention to the pattern of their conduct and its results. In the chapter, that reflection is meant to lead to action: going up, bringing wood, and building the house.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying every bad harvest proves someone has neglected God?
questions.answer: No. Haggai makes that connection in this specific address to this specific community about the neglected house of Yahweh. The chapter does not give a universal method for explaining every person’s poverty, crop failure, or frustration.

questions.question: Why are the people’s own houses mentioned so sharply?
questions.answer: The chapter sets their paneled houses beside Yahweh’s house that lies waste. Verse 9 repeats the contrast: each person is busy with his own house while Yahweh’s house lies waste. The point is the priority revealed by what they have built and what they have left undone.

questions.question: How do the people respond to Haggai’s message?
questions.answer: Zerubbabel, Joshua, and all the remnant of the people obey Yahweh’s voice and the words of Haggai. The chapter also says the people feared Yahweh. Their response is then followed by an assurance from Yahweh and by the beginning of work.

questions.question: What does “I am with you” do in the chapter?
questions.answer: It is Yahweh’s message to the people after they obey. The assurance does not replace the work; it stands between their response and the report that they came and worked on the house. The chapter presents presence and action together.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end with another date?
questions.answer: The final verse dates the start of the work to the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month in Darius’s second year. That date shows that the chapter has moved from the initial message to an actual response within the same month. It also prepares the reader to follow the book’s later dated messages.

glossary.def: The Persian king whose second regnal year dates the message and the beginning of work in this chapter.
The title given to Zerubbabel, identifying his public leadership role in Judah.
The title given to Joshua son of Jehozadak, identifying his priestly leadership role.
The people of Judah addressed with their leaders and later described as obeying and coming to work.
The withheld rain and fruitfulness Yahweh says he called on the land, crops, livestock, and labor.
